messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Fatima is a sixty-nine-year-old woman of Lebanese descent who has been married for over forty years and works the morning shift at a fast food restaurant in a mid-sized American city. She was referred for psychological assessment following a prolonged stalking ordeal that lasted nearly fourteen months and ended only when her stalker was finally arrested. She presents with a PCL-5 score of 76, indicating severe posttraumatic symptomatology, and she arrived at her first session wearing dark sunglasses she did not remove, sitting with her back to the wall.

The stalking began quietly, the way such things often do. A man she recognized vaguely from her neighborhood began appearing near her workplace, then outside her home, then sending notes through her car's windshield wiper. Over the following months, what had seemed like a peculiar coincidence calcified into something unmistakably predatory. He would wait in the parking lot of the restaurant where Fatima worked, visible through the plate glass window as she moved between the counter and the fryer. She remembers the smell of hot oil and synthetic meat as inseparable from the dread of looking up and finding him there. That smell — the ordinary, industrial smell of her workplace — became saturated with threat in a way she could not explain and could not escape, because she returned to that same restaurant every morning. Even now, months after the arrest, when Fatima ties on her apron and the ventilation pulls that warm greasy air across her face, something in her body responds before her mind has caught up, and she is briefly back in the worst of it.

The memory itself is fractured in ways that trouble her. She can recall specific moments with sensory vividness — the smell, the quality of afternoon light through the restaurant window, the exact font of one of his notes — but at other times the whole episode recedes into a strange emotional blankness, as though she is reading about a woman she has never met. She describes this dissociated recall as almost more frightening than the vivid kind, because it makes the experience feel unreal, like something too extreme to have genuinely happened to her. This unreality, in turn, feeds back into her appraisals: if she cannot fully believe it happened, she cannot trust her own judgment about whether it is truly over, and that uncertainty keeps her threat perception perpetually elevated.

What has come to dominate Fatima's daily life is a conviction, arrived at slowly and now deeply entrenched, that people fundamentally cannot be trusted. She had come to believe this not abstractly but personally — that she had been naive, that she had failed to see what was in front of her, that she no longer recognized herself as someone capable of reading the world accurately. This loss of self-recognition is not a minor complaint; she speaks of it with a quiet grief, as though the woman she was before the stalking has not returned. These appraisals — of the world as dangerous and of herself as compromised — drive her hypervigilance with a logic that feels, to her, entirely rational. At the restaurant, she watches the faces of every customer who approaches the counter, scanning for the particular stillness she learned to associate with her stalker's expression. She checks the locks on the restaurant's back door repeatedly before her shift ends, and at home she wakes two or three times each night to verify that the doors and windows are secured, lying awake afterward with her heart still working.

The loop tightens in the small hours. The waking and checking confirms to Fatima that danger is real and close; the confirmation of threat reinforces her belief that she cannot trust appearances or her own composure; and when those beliefs press too hard, she pulls back from the memory entirely, certain that if she were to sit with it fully she would not survive the feeling. That avoidance keeps the memory unprocessed and strange, which in turn sustains the sense that something monstrous and unresolved is still circling her life.

What finally brought her to seek help was her husband's quiet, worried observation that she had not laughed in months. What she is most afraid of is that this is simply who she is now. What she is most hoping, though she would not quite say it aloud, is that she is wrong.
